newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian politics hit by new turn in bribes probes.
newsitem.headline: Belgian politics hit by new turn in bribes probes.

text.p: Belgium's political landscape was rocked by new revelations in two long-running bribes probes on Friday which could prompt fresh calls from opposition groups for the country's government to step down.

Philippe Busquin, Chairman of the French-speaking Socialist Party (PS), acknowledged for the first time the party had contacts with two firms at the centre of allegations about illegal party financing.
The so-called Dassault and Agusta scandals centre on claims the French and Italian companies of the same names paid kickbacks to Belgian parties in the late 1980s to win lucrative defence contracts.
Both firms have consistently denied any wrongdoing. Belgium did not restrict corporate funding of political parties until 1989 and only banned it completely in 1993.
Busquin, who took over the reins of the PS in 1992, told a news conference he was unaware of any illegal payments.
He said, however, that following a police search of the party's headquarters on Thursday he had learned the party did receive funds from Dassault in 1987.

"I have just found out, following the raids that took place yesterday, that we received a legal gift from Dassault of 1.2 million (Belgian) francs...which was entered into our books and declared to the finance ministry in 1987," Busquin said.

Busquin also acknowledged meeting Agusta representatives in February 1988. Later the same year the company won a contract to supply the army with 46 helicopters, a deal which is also being scrutinised by police.

The inquiries into the Agusta contract led in 1994 to the resignation of three former PS ministers and in 1995 to that of NATO Secretary General Willy Claes, a member of the PS's Flemish sister party, the SP, which it is alleged also may have received kickbacks. No charges have been brought against them.
Busquin said his meeting with Agusta officials was "purely professional" in his then capacity as a regional minister representing local firms hoping to win a slice of the contract.

He added that, although in May 1988 he became a member of the federal government that chose the Italian firm in preference to offers from French and American companies, "I was never involved in any discussions inside the PS about Agusta...nor of the cabinet committee that discussed the contract".

The present PS leadership has been under pressure to clarify what it knows about party financing in the 1980s ever since the arrest last month of two party officials, said by their lawyers to have accepted 30 million Belgian francs (about $1 million) from Dassault, rekindled the bribes probes.

The coalition government has so far stuck together in the face of opposition calls for the PS to pull out. Last week the government easily defeated motions of no confidence brought against it in Parliament.
